design_rules: Species describe biological constraints and broad historical traditions, not individual personality.
No civilization is culturally uniform; these entries describe widespread patterns recognizable across known space.
Modern port culture has been shaped by generations of multispecies contact.
Translation is mature but names, technical jargon, humor and social assumptions still carry cultural differences.

cultures.identity: Highly pluralistic; outsiders often find the absence of one authoritative Human way of doing something more characteristic than any particular custom.

names.pattern: Naming traditions remain extremely diverse and usually reflect inherited Earth cultures, colonial history or family preference.
names.usage: Given name plus family name is common in interstellar commercial records, but software must support many other structures.

cultures.households: Nuclear families, extended families, communal households and chosen-family arrangements all occur. Offworld colonies often revive multigenerational households because housing and childcare are expensive.
food: Portable breads, coffee/tea traditions and preserved comfort foods spread unusually well through freight culture.
Human food is widely available at multispecies ports because Human carriers expanded aggressively.
cultures.clothing: Work clothing tends toward pockets, layered climate protection and standardized PPE. Fashion varies too much for a single recognizable civilian style.
cultures.architecture: Human commercial construction is modular but inconsistent. Additions, retrofits and competing manufacturers are normal.
cultures.work_culture: Strong tradition of independent contractors, small carriers and improvisation alongside enormous corporations.
shipboard_customs: Naming ships is nearly universal but naming conventions vary wildly.
Captains frequently personalize bridges and common areas with objects that have no operational purpose.
Improvised repairs may remain installed long after the emergency ends.
etiquette: Eye contact has culturally variable meanings even among Humans.
Visitors are often expected to ask rather than assume household rules.
cultures.death: Practices remain culturally and religiously diverse. Space settlements commonly support memorial services even when remains are returned elsewhere.

views_of_others.kesh: Admiration for durability, jokes about mass.
views_of_others.ilyan: Admiration for elegant engineering, occasional frustration with tolerances.
views_of_others.vey: Strong association with excellent environmental systems.
views_of_others.orun: Respect for maintainability mixed with Human discomfort about some communal-space norms.

cultures.identity: A high-gravity civilization whose institutions tend to value demonstrated reliability, continuity and responsibility for things placed in one's care.

names.pattern: Most Kesh use a personal name followed by a lineage or household identifier in formal contexts.
names.usage: Commercial acquaintances generally shorten to the personal name after introduction.

cultures.households: Extended households are common and may include several generations plus long-term non-kin members. A household is partly a social unit and partly a network of obligations.
food: Dense high-calorie meals are common on Keshar.
Stews, pressed grain dishes, shallow-sea proteins and heavily roasted foods travel well.
Kesh often find low-gravity portions visually generous but nutritionally unsatisfying.
cultures.clothing: Close-fitting durable garments avoid snagging around heavy machinery. Ceremonial clothing uses layered textiles and metal or ceramic household pieces.
cultures.architecture: Broad spans, low centers of mass, obvious load paths and extremely robust handholds. Furniture built for Kesh can be comically heavy elsewhere.
cultures.work_culture: Maintenance is a moral as well as technical responsibility. Signing off unsafe work carries serious stigma. Apprenticeship traditions remain strong even in advanced industries.
shipboard_customs: A new chief engineer traditionally performs a complete physical walk-through rather than accepting records alone.
Temporary repairs are marked conspicuously until properly resolved.
Kesh crews dislike inaccessible equipment even when reliability statistics say access is rarely needed.
etiquette: Promises stated plainly are treated seriously; casual overpromising reads as irresponsibility.
Offering physical assistance without being asked can imply that someone appears incapable, though frontier practice is looser.
cultures.death: Households commonly preserve an object associated with the deceased's work or daily responsibilities. Industrial communities maintain unusually detailed memorial records of fatal accidents.

views_of_others.human: Resourceful and occasionally alarmingly willing to improvise.
views_of_others.ilyan: Technically impressive but sometimes designed too close to minimum margins.
views_of_others.vey: Trusted in environmental systems where failure is unacceptable.
views_of_others.orun: Familiar respect for maintainability, though Kesh prefer more physical separation between living and machinery.

cultures.identity: Low gravity shaped a civilization attentive to mass, balance, spatial efficiency and the cost of carrying unnecessary things.

names.pattern: Personal names are typically short; a second name often indicates family, place or professional lineage.
names.usage: Titles are used sparingly outside formal institutions.

cultures.households: Households often occupy vertically distributed spaces that other species perceive as inconveniently separated. Kinship is important, but young adults commonly spend extended periods in educational or professional residences.
food: Light meals eaten frequently are common.
Aerated breads, climbing vines, fruiting plants and small cultivated proteins feature prominently.
Heavy high-fat Kesh food has a devoted minority following and a reputation for ending productivity for the day.
cultures.clothing: Light layered garments and harness-compatible workwear. Decorative textiles emphasize motion and drape in low gravity.
cultures.architecture: Height is cheap. Cities use towers, suspended walkways and long vertical transit shafts. Rooms designed for Ilyan often feel narrow to Kesh.
cultures.work_culture: Precision and preparation are valued because unnecessary mass and rework are seen as avoidable costs. Tool control aboard spacecraft is particularly strict.
shipboard_customs: Mass manifests are treated with near-accounting seriousness.
Loose personal objects underway are considered poor seamanship.
Engine rooms tend to be visually sparse but densely instrumented.
etiquette: Interrupting a careful technical explanation is often taken more negatively than open disagreement.
Complimenting efficiency is more meaningful than calling something beautiful in many professional settings.
cultures.death: Memorial traditions frequently emphasize what a person taught, designed or enabled others to accomplish rather than preservation of possessions.

views_of_others.human: Inventive, adaptable and astonishingly tolerant of redundant objects.
views_of_others.orun: Ingenious packaging; sometimes socially intense for Ilyan accustomed to more spatial separation.

cultures.identity: A semi-aquatic civilization in which environmental stewardship, water systems and shared ecological consequences became foundational social assumptions.

names.pattern: Names commonly have a personal form and a longer formal form associated with family/community waters.
names.usage: Offworld records usually use a shortened two-part form because full traditional forms can encode geographic relationships.

cultures.households: Households historically clustered around shared water access and remain somewhat more communal than typical Human households. Childcare and meals often cross household boundaries.
food: Aquatic proteins, algae, fermented marine plants and broth-like dishes are common.
Vey cuisine adapted well to shipboard hydroponics and closed-cycle aquaculture.
cultures.clothing: Quick-drying fabrics, wraps and garments that tolerate high humidity. Offworld work clothing includes skin-moisture management layers in dry environments.
cultures.architecture: Water circulation is visible rather than hidden. Public spaces may include shallow channels, humid gardens and immersion areas alongside dry visitor routes.
cultures.work_culture: Environmental systems are treated as infrastructure everyone should understand at least minimally. Waste streams are routinely considered inputs to another process.
shipboard_customs: Water-quality status is commonly displayed as prominently as reactor status.
Vey crews tend to notice smells, humidity shifts and airflow changes before instrumentation alarms.
Shared wash/immersion facilities can surprise species with stronger privacy conventions.
etiquette: Offering water is a basic hospitality gesture with more social weight than it carries in many Human cultures.
Wastefulness involving clean water can provoke a surprisingly emotional response even where water is abundant.
cultures.death: Many traditions return biological material to managed ecosystems after ceremonial treatment; offworld communities maintain symbolic equivalents where local biosphere rules prevent it.

views_of_others.human: Energetic and adaptable, but historically careless with environmental externalities.
views_of_others.kesh: Reliable partners whose systems are easy to trust.
views_of_others.orun: Strong shared understanding that habitation and infrastructure are one system.

cultures.identity: Descended from communal burrowers, Orun civilization generally treats proximity, shared infrastructure and visible maintenance as ordinary rather than intrusive.

names.pattern: Personal names are commonly paired with a community or junction name rather than a hereditary family surname.
names.usage: Offworld forms often compress the connector, producing records such as Ruun Keshet.

cultures.households: The boundary between household and neighborhood is less rigid than for most species. Private sleeping spaces exist, but cooking, work and recreation are frequently communal.
food: Roasted tubers, fungi, subterranean-grown greens and mineral-rich broths are common.
Communal cooking vessels remain culturally important.
Strong temperature contrasts in food are popular.
cultures.clothing: Compact durable garments suited to crawling, climbing and working in tight service spaces. Personal decoration often appears on belts, tool carriers and collars rather than loose garments.
cultures.architecture: Networks rather than rooms. Habitation, transit and machinery interpenetrate; dead-end corridors are uncommon. Acoustic privacy requires deliberate construction.
cultures.work_culture: Maintenance knowledge is widely distributed. A worker saying 'not my system' during an obvious failure is viewed poorly even outside their formal job.
shipboard_customs: Access panels are expected to open without dismantling finished interiors.
Crew commonly perform minor maintenance while socializing.
Orun-built ships often have multiple crawl routes around critical machinery.
etiquette: Silence in a shared space does not imply a desire to be left alone.
Closing a door can carry a stronger privacy signal than other species expect; polite visitors take it seriously.
cultures.death: Communities often preserve maps or diagrams marking places a deceased member built, repaired or inhabited. Names may remain attached to junctions for generations.

views_of_others.kesh: Easy to work beside; both cultures respect physical infrastructure.
views_of_others.ilyan: Excellent design discipline but too much empty separation in some habitats.
views_of_others.vey: Deeply compatible ideas about shared systems and collective maintenance.
